302.title: Starting again
302.hook: refugee Sikh families rebuild from nothing in Delhi, East Punjab and beyond
302.howItsDone: Sikhs close the Ardas by asking for chardi kala, rising spirits, and many families from Partition speak of it together with kirat karni, honest work, when they tell how they rebuilt.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Partition: a line through Punjab, millions crossing, Nankana Sahib left on the other side. Your line was a land split in two. So what do you do the morning after you've lost everything? Day three hundred two.

A refugee train pulls into Delhi in the autumn of 1947, and a family climbs down with a bundle of clothes, a few pots and a brass water jug from home. Back home they had a farm, or a shop, or a house with a courtyard. Now they have a tent in a refugee camp and a number on a list. The father finds a cart and sells whatever he can buy cheap that morning. The mother takes in sewing. The children go to school under a tree. It will take years. Some families will tell you it took a generation. Today: starting again.
screen: `A BUNDLE, A FEW POTS.` → `A TENT AND A NUMBER.` → `A CART, A NEEDLE, A SCHOOL UNDER A TREE.`

segments.voice: Start with the camps. In Delhi there was Kingsway Camp; near Kurukshetra, a huge camp of tents that held a city's worth of people. Hindu and Sikh refugees from the west lived in them for months, some for years. Then the building began. Whole new neighborhoods went up in Delhi for refugee families, and you can still hear Punjabi from the older shops there. In East Punjab, families who had left farms were given land against what they'd lost, often less, and often worse, than what they left behind. They cleared it and planted anyway. Many moved on again, to other cities, and later across the world. Now the Sikh word underneath all of this. You learned it early on the path: chardi kala. Chardi means rising, climbing. Kala is spirit, strength. Rising spirits, an unbeaten heart. It is said at the end of every Ardas, and it doesn't mean pretending things are fine. The families of 1947 grieved. Many never spoke about what they saw. Chardi kala is grief and getting up at the same time. It sits beside another old teaching, kirat karni, earning an honest living with your own hands. A cart is honest work. So is a needle. So is a small shop. Families still tell stories of a grandfather who started over late in life with nothing but that. The line today has one extra word: again. Chardi kala isn't a mood you find once. It's something you choose again, the next morning, and the next.
screen: `THE CAMPS: KINGSWAY, KURUKSHETRA.` · `NEW HOMES, NEW FIELDS.` · `CHARDI KALA: RISING SPIRITS.` · `GRIEF AND GETTING UP, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `CHARDI KALA, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin one small thing again. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you let go of. A walk you used to take. A letter you meant to write. A few lines of reading. A habit that slipped when life got hard. Don't scold yourself about why it stopped. Just pick it up in your mind, the way you'd pick up a tool. Decide the smallest possible first step, one you could take today. Then rest with the breath, and let the decision settle. The bell holds the time.
Starting again. Refugee families of 1947 rebuilt from nothing, in tents, carts and new fields, with chardi kala: rising spirits, chosen again each day.
Your line: chardi kala, again. Today, take the first small step of that thing you're starting again, even if it takes two minutes. Day three hundred two.

303.title: A Punjabi-speaking state, 1966
303.hook: after long campaigning, a smaller Punjab is formed around the Punjabi language
303.tomorrow: The daily prayer for open doors
303.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Punjabi Suba movement as a long, largely peaceful campaign; many gurdwaras still teach Gurmukhi so that Punjabi, the language of the Guru Granth Sahib's script, is kept.

segments.voice: Yesterday, starting again: tents, carts, new fields, and your line, chardi kala, again. Did you take that first small step? Today the rebuilding turns to something you can't carry in a bundle: a language. Day three hundred three.

Some words don't survive translation. A grandmother's scolding, in the language she grew up with. A family's private switch of tongue when the kids shouldn't follow. The name of a dish. The way people say goodbye at the door. A language carries all of that, which is why people will campaign for years to keep one. In the 1950s, India's map was being redrawn around languages, state by state. Punjabi speakers asked for a state of their own, and were told no. Today: a Punjabi-speaking state.
screen: `WORDS THAT DON'T TRANSLATE.` → `THE MAP REDRAWN BY LANGUAGE.` → `PUNJABI SPEAKERS TOLD NO.`

segments.voice: After independence, India began reorganizing its states around the languages people spoke. Telugu speakers got a state. So did others. But when Sikh leaders asked for a state built around Punjabi, the answer was no, for years. The campaign was called the Punjabi Suba movement, suba meaning a province. It was led by the Akali Dal, first under Master Tara Singh and later under Sant Fateh Singh. Its main tool was the morcha: a peaceful campaign in which volunteers marched, sang and courted arrest, wave after wave. Tens of thousands went to jail. Language had become tangled with religion and politics. Punjabi written in Gurmukhi, the script of the Guru Granth Sahib, was close to Sikh hearts. In the censuses of those years, many Punjabi-speaking Hindus, urged on by some Hindu organizations, recorded Hindi as their language instead. So the question was never only about grammar. Then, in 1966, after the war with Pakistan the year before, the government agreed. On the first of November 1966, Punjab was divided again, this time peacefully. The Hindi-speaking south became a new state, Haryana. Hill districts went to Himachal Pradesh. What remained was a smaller Punjab, with Punjabi in Gurmukhi as its language, and with Chandigarh held back as a shared capital. Not everyone was satisfied. Arguments over Chandigarh and the river waters went on for decades, and they matter for the harder chapters ahead. But the thing that was kept was the language itself: offices, street signs and school books in Punjabi, written in the script of the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say a word in your first language. Settle, and breathe. Find one word from the language you grew up with, or the one your family spoke before you. Maybe a word for grandmother, or bread, or home. Say it quietly, once. Notice where it lands in your body, and who it brings to mind. If you only have one language, find a word that belongs to your family alone, a nickname, a saying. Then rest with the breath and let that word keep you company. The bell holds the time.
Punjabi suba. The movement for a Punjabi-speaking province, which won, on November 1, 1966, a smaller Punjab with Punjabi in Gurmukhi as its language.
Your line: the language kept. Today, ask someone older what a word from their first language means to them, and let them teach it to you. Day three hundred three.

304.title: The daily prayer for open doors
304.hook: for decades the Ardas asked for free access to the gurdwaras left behind
304.howItsDone: In the Ardas, said standing at the close of most Sikh gatherings, Sikhs ask for open access to, and the care of, Nankana Sahib and the other gurdwaras from which the Panth was separated in 1947.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjabi suba: a smaller Punjab, won by peaceful morchas, and your line, the language kept. Today we go back to 1947 one more time, to something Sikhs carried out of it into every single day. Day three hundred four.

A childhood house someone else lives in now. A grandparent's town across an ocean. A front door remembered exactly, that can't be walked through. For Sikhs after 1947, that door was Nankana Sahib, where Guru Nanak was born, and many other gurdwaras now across a border. The community did not keep that longing for one anniversary a year. It put it into the prayer said every day. Today: the daily prayer for open doors.
screen: `A DOOR YOU CAN'T WALK THROUGH.` → `NANKANA SAHIB, ACROSS THE BORDER.` → `A LONGING PUT INTO A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: You've met the Ardas already: the standing prayer that closes nearly every Sikh gathering. It's said standing, hands joined, facing the Guru Granth Sahib. It remembers the ten Gurus, then the Sikhs who gave their lives, then it asks. The Ardas isn't a fixed text from one day in history. Its core is old, and the community has added to it as the story went on. After Partition, a request was added. In plain English, it asks the Guru to grant the Khalsa free sight of, and the care and service of, Nankana Sahib and the other gurdwaras and holy places from which the Panth has been separated. The Punjabi phrase at its heart is khulle darshan didar: open sight, open visits. So ever since, in homes and gurdwaras around the world, Sikhs have asked, every day, for a door to open. Notice what that does. A loss that could have turned bitter became a daily hope, said out loud, together. The door was not fully shut. Groups of pilgrims, called jathas, were allowed to cross for the big gurpurabs, under agreements between India and Pakistan. But for many Sikhs, a visit to Guru Nanak's birthplace stayed a lifelong hope. Many never went. And still the line was said. The request is in the Ardas today, because Sikhs still ask for open, free access to all the places they were separated from. It's a small lesson in how a community holds a longing: not by forgetting it, and not by letting it harden, but by praying it, gently, every day.
screen: `THE ARDAS: REMEMBER, THEN ASK.` · `A REQUEST ADDED AFTER 1947.` · `KHULLE DARSHAN DIDAR: OPEN SIGHT.` · `A LOSS TURNED INTO DAILY HOPE.` · then, large: `OPEN DOORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold something you've hoped for a long time. Settle, and breathe. Let one long hope come to mind. A reconciliation. A healing. A place you want to see. A door you want opened, for you or for someone else. Don't push it or plan it. Just let it be there. If you pray, you can offer it in your own words, the way the Sikh community has offered its hope for decades. If you don't, simply name it quietly to yourself, and notice how long you've carried it. The bell holds the time.
Ardas. The standing prayer that closes nearly every Sikh gathering — since Partition, it has asked for open access to Nankana Sahib and the gurdwaras left behind: khulle darshan didar.
Your line: open doors. Today, open one door for someone else: an invitation, an introduction, a seat at your table. Day three hundred four.

305.title: Kartarpur corridor, 2019
305.hook: a corridor opens so pilgrims from India can visit Kartarpur, where Nanak farmed
305.howItsDone: Sikh pilgrims from India cross the Kartarpur corridor, when it is open, to visit Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, where Guru Nanak lived his last years; many Sikhs mark his birth anniversary there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ardas: after 1947, the Ardas began asking for open sight of the gurdwaras left behind. Your line was open doors. Today, for one of those places, the answer came. Day three hundred five.

For years, at a town called Dera Baba Nanak, right on the Indian side of the border, there was a viewing platform. Pilgrims climbed up, sometimes with binoculars, and looked across the fields. About four kilometers away, just visible on a clear day, stood a white gurdwara in Pakistan. People would stand there and bow to a building they could see but couldn't reach. Some came back year after year. Some grew old doing it. Then, in November 2019, a road opened. Today: the Kartarpur corridor.
screen: `A PLATFORM AT THE BORDER.` → `A WHITE GURDWARA, FOUR KILOMETERS AWAY.` → `NOVEMBER 2019: A ROAD OPENS.`

segments.voice: Start with the place. Kartarpur means the Creator's town. Guru Nanak founded it on the bank of the river Ravi after his long journeys, and he spent the last years of his life there, about eighteen of them. Remember what he did there: he farmed. The Guru who had spent some twenty years on the road, across India and, tradition says, as far as Mecca and Baghdad, came home and worked the fields. Around him grew the first Sikh community: people who worked honestly, sang together morning and evening, and ate together. It's where Guru Nanak passed the light to Guru Angad, and where he died, in 1539. In 1947 the border put Kartarpur on the Pakistani side, close enough to see, too far to touch. Then, in 2019, the two governments opened a corridor: a road, a bridge and a crossing, so pilgrims from India could walk to the gurdwara without a visa and come back the same day. It opened on the ninth of November, days before the five hundred fiftieth anniversary of Guru Nanak's birth. People wept at the crossing. Old men who had stood on the platform for decades walked in. It hasn't been simple. The corridor has closed at times, during the pandemic and in periods of tension between the two countries. But for Sikhs it answered, in part, the prayer said every day since 1947. And it closes our long walk through Sikh history: from Banda Singh and the years in the forests, through the Misls and Maharaja Ranjit Singh, annexation and the gurdwara reform, to Partition and a door that opened.
screen: `KARTARPUR: THE CREATOR'S TOWN.` · `WHERE NANAK FARMED AND DIED.` · `A CORRIDOR OPENS, 2019.` · `A PRAYER ANSWERED, IN PART.` · then, large: `THE DOOR OPENED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk to a place that matters. If you can, stand up and walk, even across the room, to a spot that means something: a window, a photograph, a doorway you love. If you can't move right now, walk there in your mind, step by step. As you go, notice that you are going toward something, not just away. When you arrive, stand or sit there quietly. Let yourself be glad you can reach it. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Kartarpur corridor. The road opened in November 2019 so pilgrims from India could visit Kartarpur, where Guru Nanak farmed and died, without a visa.
Your line: the door opened. Today, notice one door in your life that's open now but once was closed, and take a moment to be glad of it. Day three hundred five.

306.title: Before we begin
306.hook: this week remembers a year of deep pain for Sikhs; we go slowly and blame no people as a whole
306.howItsDone: Sikhs remember 1984 each June and November with Ardas, kirtan and gatherings; many families also speak of it privately, and gently, at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kartarpur corridor: a road to the town where Guru Nanak farmed, and your line, the door opened. That closed our walk through Sikh history. This week is different, so today we pause at the door first. Day three hundred six.

Some dates, in some families, are said more quietly than others. Ask about 1984 in some Sikh homes, and there may be a long silence before an answer. Or a story about an uncle. Or a photograph brought out from a drawer. For many Sikh families, 1984 is a wound still within living memory. It isn't a chapter in a book; it's parents, neighbors, a childhood. So before we begin this week, we're going to stop for a day and talk about how we'll walk through it. Today: before we begin.
screen: `SOME DATES ARE SAID QUIETLY.` → `1984: A WOUND IN LIVING MEMORY.` → `FIRST, HOW WE'LL WALK.`

segments.voice: Here's what this week holds. Tomorrow, Punjab in the early 1980s: how a political crisis became violent. Then June 1984, when the Indian army entered the Harmandir Sahib complex. Then a library that was lost. Then November 1984, when mobs killed thousands of Sikhs, mostly in Delhi. Then the long wait for justice, and finally how the Sikh community remembers. Now, how we'll walk. First: slowly. One piece a day. Nothing here is told for drama. Second: carefully with the facts. Numbers, causes and people from these years are still argued about. Where accounts differ, we'll say so, and keep to what is widely documented. Third, and most important: we blame no people as a whole. Governments and individuals made choices, and some committed terrible crimes. But no faith and no community is guilty as a whole. In November, there were Hindu neighbors who hid Sikh families in their homes at great risk. Sikhs themselves hold very different views about the people and choices of those years. This week asks for holding more than one thing at once. Fourth: together. The Sikh word is sangat, the company of others on the path. Grief carried alone gets heavier; carried in company, it can be held. And fifth: you may stop. If this week is too heavy for you right now, you can wait. The path will still be here. That, too, is honoring the memory: coming to it when you can give it your full attention.
screen: `WHAT THIS WEEK HOLDS.` · `SLOWLY, AND CAREFUL WITH FACTS.` · `NO PEOPLE AS A WHOLE TO BLAME.` · `TOGETHER, AND FREE TO WAIT.` · then, large: `GENTLY, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe, and then choose. Settle, and take a few slow breaths. Notice how you feel, right now, about going into this week. Curious? Heavy? Unsure? Whatever it is, it's allowed. Then make a quiet choice. Continue tomorrow, or wait a while and come back. Either choice is fine, and nobody is keeping score. If you do continue, you might decide now who you'd talk to if something weighs on you. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Sangat. The company of others on the path — before this painful week begins, we go slowly, keep to what is documented, and blame no people as a whole.
Your line: gently, together. Today, when someone brings up something painful, slow down, listen first, and let them set the pace. Day three hundred six.

307.title: Punjab in the early 1980s
307.hook: political demands, rising violence and armed militants inside the Harmandir complex, led by Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, a figure Sikhs see very differently, brought crisis
307.howItsDone: Sikhs hold a range of views on the early 1980s and on Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale; in gurdwaras and families these years are usually discussed with care, and often with strong feeling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sangat: slowly, carefully with the facts, no people as a whole to blame. Your line was gently, together. If you've chosen to continue, here is the first piece: how the crisis grew. Day three hundred seven.

Some arguments start with something real: money, fairness, who gets a say. Nobody listens. Voices rise. A door slams. Then something happens that can't be taken back, and years later everyone involved tells the story differently, each holding a true piece of it. Punjab at the start of the 1980s was something like that, but with a whole state, a national government and many lives at stake. Today: Punjab in the early 1980s.
screen: `AN ARGUMENT THAT STARTS WITH SOMETHING REAL.` → `NOBODY LISTENS.` → `EVERYONE HOLDS A TRUE PIECE.`

segments.voice: It began with politics. In 1973 the Akali Dal, the main Sikh party, passed the Anandpur Sahib Resolution, asking for more power for the states and for Chandigarh to be Punjab's. By the early 1980s, a fair share of Punjab's river waters was among the demands too. Governments in Delhi saw some of it as a threat to the nation. Talks went nowhere. In 1982 the Akalis began a new morcha, and tens of thousands of Sikhs courted arrest. Into this stepped Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, the head of a traditional Sikh school, the Damdami Taksal. He was a powerful preacher. He called Sikhs back to amrit, to their practice, away from drink and drugs, and he spoke fiercely about injustice to Sikhs. Meanwhile, violence grew in Punjab. There were killings of Hindus, of Sikhs who disagreed, of police, and hard police action in return. From 1982 Bhindranwale lived inside the Harmandir Sahib complex, and in December 1983 he and armed followers moved into the Akal Takht, which was fortified in the months that followed. Here is where we must hold the whole story. Sikhs see Bhindranwale very differently. Some honor him as a saint and a martyr who stood up for a community they felt was treated unjustly. Other Sikhs believe his path, and weapons in the holiest place, led to disaster. The Indian government called him a terrorist. People in Punjab of every faith lived in fear in those years. This lesson doesn't settle who was right. It asks you to hold the demands, the grievances, the violence and the fear all at once, because they were all there.
screen: `THE DEMANDS: POWER, WATER, A CAPITAL.` · `A PREACHER CALLS SIKHS BACK.` · `VIOLENCE GROWS, AND FORTIFICATION.` · `SIKHS SEE HIM VERY DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `HOLD THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with complexity, not sides. Settle, and breathe. Think of a conflict you know, in your family, your town or the news, where people you respect disagree. Picture one person from each side. Let each tell you, in your mind, what they're afraid of. Don't decide who wins. Just notice that fear and hurt live on both sides of most arguments. If you feel yourself taking a side, gently widen the frame again. The bell holds the time.
Morcha. A peaceful campaign of protest — in the early 1980s, amid political demands, rising violence, and armed militants in the Harmandir complex, around a leader Sikhs see very differently.
Your line: hold the whole story. Today, when you hear one side of any conflict, ask yourself quietly what the other side is afraid of. Day three hundred seven.

308.title: June 1984
308.hook: the Indian army stormed the Harmandir complex during the martyrdom gurpurab of Guru Arjan; the Akal Takht was badly damaged and many pilgrims died
308.howItsDone: Each June, Sikhs gather at the Akal Takht and in gurdwaras worldwide for Ardas and kirtan in remembrance of those who died in 1984, and many light lamps or hold vigils.

segments.voice: Yesterday, morcha: demands, violence, fear, and a leader Sikhs see very differently. Your line was hold the whole story. Today, the week's hardest day. Go gently. Day three hundred eight.

Early June, in Amritsar, is hot. In 1984 it was also the time of a gurpurab: the day Sikhs mark the martyrdom of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, who compiled the scripture and was put to death in Lahore. Families came to the Harmandir Sahib for it. Grandparents. Children. Villagers who'd saved for the trip. Many of them had nothing to do with politics. They came to bow, to listen to kirtan by the water, to eat langar. And they were inside the complex when the army came. Today: June 1984.
screen: `EARLY JUNE: GURU ARJAN'S MARTYRDOM DAY.` → `FAMILIES COME TO THE HARMANDIR.` → `THEY WERE INSIDE.`

segments.voice: The government ordered the army to remove the armed militants from the complex. The operation was called Blue Star. A curfew was imposed across Punjab, and at the beginning of June the army surrounded the Harmandir Sahib. After days of firing, on the night of the fifth and sixth of June, troops entered, and tanks were used against the Akal Takht, where Bhindranwale and his fighters had fortified themselves. The Akal Takht, the seat of Sikh authority founded by Guru Hargobind, was badly damaged. Bhindranwale was killed. So were many soldiers. And so were many pilgrims, caught inside. How many died is disputed. The government's own count was several hundred militants and civilians, and eighty-three soldiers. Many Sikhs, and many independent accounts, believe the true number was far higher, in the thousands, and that many of the dead were ordinary worshipers. Other gurdwaras across Punjab were entered at the same time. For Sikhs in Punjab and far beyond, it was a deep shock: the Harmandir Sahib had been attacked, on a holy day. Sikh remembrance at the Akal Takht calls it the third ghallughara, the third great massacre, after the two of the 1700s you learned about earlier. Afterward, the government repaired the Akal Takht itself. Sikhs refused that repair, took it down, and rebuilt it with their own hands, through kar seva, voluntary service. Looking back over this week: starting again, a language kept, a prayer for open doors, a door opened, a pause, a crisis, and now this. Today we remember above all the pilgrims.
screen: `OPERATION BLUE STAR.` · `THE AKAL TAKHT BADLY DAMAGED.` · `HOW MANY DIED IS DISPUTED.` · `THE THIRD GHALLUGHARA.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE PILGRIMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a lamp for those who died. If you have a candle or a small lamp, and it's safe, light it now. If not, picture one: a small flame, steady. Let it stand for the pilgrims who came for a holy day, and for everyone who died that June. You don't need names. Just keep your eyes on the flame, or on the picture of it, and breathe slowly. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer. If you don't, let the flame do the remembering. The bell holds the time.
Ghallughara. A great massacre — what many Sikhs call June 1984, the third, when the army entered the Harmandir complex and the Akal Takht was badly damaged.
Your line: remember the pilgrims. Today, think of the ordinary people in any hard story you hear, the ones who were just there, and keep them in mind. Day three hundred eight.

fork.reveal: Sikhs refused the government's repair and rebuilt the Akal Takht with their own hands, as voluntary service.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ghallughara, a great massacre; many Sikhs call June 1984 the third, after 1746 and 1762.

trapdoor: what you thought: an army operation against armed men.
what it means: an attack on the holiest Sikh place on a holy day, in which many pilgrims died.
what a scholar hears: the government's white paper gave 493 militants and civilians and 83 soldiers killed; many Sikh and independent estimates are far higher.
